clue.text: Scottish simpleton is annoying, having switched sides

indicators.note: the two sides of a word are its ends, so its first and last letters change places

blocks.note: to hump is a colloquial verb meaning to annoy or vex, so 'is annoying' gives this form

explanation.surface: Someone complains that a slow-witted Scotsman is tiresome since he defected to the other team.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the outer letters swap; the middle UMP stays put.
explanation.definitionFit: Sumph is a Scots word for a dull, stupid fellow, a dolt.

clue.text: Lecturer housed in smart joint

indicators.note: something housed in another is lodged inside it, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: spiff is a colloquial adjective meaning smart or dapper
L is the standard abbreviation for lecturer

explanation.surface: An academic is put up in a stylish pub or eatery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' looks like a restaurant or premises; it is the slang cannabis cigarette.
explanation.definitionFit: A spliff is slang for a hand-rolled cannabis cigarette, also called a joint.

clue.text: Homeland forms setting for this Hindu festival

indicators.note: the word forms a setting, a mount around a jewel, so the solution sits inside its letters

blocks.note: the middle letters of this word

explanation.surface: A Hindu festival is held in its home country.
explanation.definitionFit: A mela is a Hindu fair or religious festival, such as the Kumbh Mela.

clue.text: How does Welsh so-and-so sound? He might have been promising

indicators.note: asking how a word sounds in a Welsh mouth means we want its pronunciation in that accent

blocks.note: a so-and-so is a blighter; stage Welsh, like Fluellen in Henry V, turns B into P

explanation.surface: A question about a Welsh rascal's speech, and a hint that he once showed promise.
explanation.walkthrough: The comic Welsh accent of English literature hardens B to P, so the blighter becomes something else.
explanation.definitionFit: To plight is to pledge, so a plighter is one who makes a promise, such as a betrothal vow.

clue.text: It's very hard taking in wild cat breed

indicators.note: something wild is out of control, so these letters run in a disordered way
taking something in means admitting it inside, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: HH is the pencil grading for very hard lead
the three letters jumbled

explanation.surface: A hard task is reared up in trying to tame and breed feral cats.
explanation.definitionFit: To hatch is to bring young out of eggs, to breed or produce offspring.

clue.text: What young couples are after? Newly built in Herts, most are (12, two words)

indicators.note: a thing newly built is constructed afresh, so these letters are put together in a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Couples seeking a first house find most in Hertfordshire are new builds.
explanation.walkthrough: Herts is the abbreviation for Hertfordshire, a county north of London; the surface fits the anagram so well it nearly reads as a definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Starter homes are small first properties aimed at young buyers getting on the housing ladder.

clue.text: Uniformed collaborateurs, not quite benign reserve

indicators.note: not quite means falling a little short, so the final letter of the word is dropped

blocks.note: mild means gentle or benign
ice is reserve or coldness of manner

explanation.surface: Members of a uniformed collaborationist force are described as not quite kindly and rather aloof.
explanation.definitionFit: The Milice was the paramilitary police of Vichy France, which collaborated with the Nazi occupiers.

clue.text: If prime suffers and concretion follows, this can cause termination

indicators.note: a thing that suffers is damaged and knocked out of shape, so the letters before it are rearranged

blocks.note: taken letter for letter
a stone is a hard concretion, as in a kidney stone

explanation.surface: A medical warning: a patient in their prime suffers, a hard lump forms, and the outcome is ended.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Follows' places the stone after the reworked letters; 'termination' is the medical sense, ending a pregnancy.
explanation.definitionFit: Mifepristone is the drug used for medical abortion, blocking progesterone so a pregnancy ends.

clue.text: Part of what airline's taken up, organization of major carriers

indicators.note: only a part of the following words is wanted, a run of letters inside them
in a down entry, taking something up lifts it from bottom to top, so it reads backwards

blocks.note: letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: Part of what an airline has adopted comes from the body of big carriers.
explanation.definitionFit: IATA, the International Air Transport Association, is the trade body of the world's airlines.

clue.text: Blackening appearance (say) of popular ruler

blocks.note: in means fashionable or popular
a king is a ruler

explanation.walkthrough: 'Appearance (say)' hints that the answer, written as two words, looks like a phrase describing a well-liked monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Inking is covering with ink, so blackening something with it.

clue.text: Hairpiece in Shakespeare I put over velvety stuff

blocks.note: che is the Somerset dialect form of I used by Edgar in King Lear
velure is an old word for velvet or a velvety fabric, used by Shakespeare

explanation.definitionFit: A chevelure is a head of hair, and by extension a wig or periwig.

clue.text: King in grip of old injury returning went off the rails

R for rex, Latin for king

explanation.definitionFit: To err is to go astray or make a mistake, figuratively to leave the rails.

clue.text: Untidy altar with pile belonging to senior churchman

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

clue.text: Precocious minx indeed, accepting love bed in Paris

blocks.note: la is an old exclamation of emphasis or surprise, indeed

lit is French for bed

clue.text: Search in Glasgow: a —— is one posing questions

explanation.walkthrough: Reading the blank and the article together, 'a' plus the answer makes a word for a questioner.
explanation.definitionFit: Sker is a Scots dialect verb meaning to search or scour, given in Chambers.

clue.text: Man circling the earth turned up hellish place

indicators.note: circling something means going round it, so the first word surrounds the second
in a down entry, turned up means flipped bottom to top, read backwards

blocks.note: a man is a male
the globe is the earth

clue.text: Advertising ideas man turning life around among Native Americans

a thing placed among others is set in their midst, inside them

the Cree are a Native American people

explanation.definitionFit: In advertising a creative is a noun for the person who devises copy and concepts.

clue.text: Trouble in the Gorbals has dispersed following fine

indicators.note: something dispersed is scattered, so the word's letters are spread into a new order

the three letters jumbled

explanation.definitionFit: Fash is Scots for to trouble or bother, as in 'dinna fash yersel'.

clue.text: Lively dance, very merry?

indicators.note: lively letters jump about, so the word that follows is rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An energetic dance leaves everyone in high spirits.

explanation.definitionFit: Caned is British slang for heavily intoxicated by drink or drugs, a euphemistic step beyond merry.

clue.text: Cordial group one leads in climbing volcano

indicators.note: one that leads goes in front, so the single letter comes ahead of the group
in a down entry climbing means going upwards, so the word is read from bottom to top
placed in means set inside the other word

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral one
a set is a group
Etna is the Sicilian volcano

explanation.surface: A friendly band, led by one person, ascends a volcano.
explanation.definitionFit: Anisette is a sweet aniseed-flavoured liqueur, and cordial is an old word for such a liqueur.

clue.text: Downright excited to receive HM, with much sweet talk?

indicators.note: to receive something is to take it in, so the second word holds the abbreviation inside

blocks.note: flat means outright or downright, as in a flat refusal
tingly means thrilled or excited
HM, Her Majesty, is ER, Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: Someone thrilled to host the Queen lays the compliments on thick.
explanation.definitionFit: Flatteringly means in a manner full of compliments and praise, which is sweet talk.

clue.text: Flashy costumier crazed with ire

indicators.note: something crazed is cracked all over, so its letters are broken up and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A showy costume-maker driven mad with anger.
explanation.definitionFit: Meretricious means superficially attractive but cheap and tawdry, gaudy or showy.

clue.text: Cork replaced with bits of early Turkish carpeting

indicators.note: bits of the words means only a small piece of each, here their opening letter
replaced means put back in a different arrangement, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written
the initials of the two words

explanation.definitionFit: A rocket is British slang for a severe reprimand, the same as a carpeting from the boss.

clue.text: Expression always appearing in chorus

an ort is a scrap of food left over from a meal

clue.text: Siren maybe, cheeky first to last

clue.text: Feeling vexed when cha's off? Don't look so miserable

clue.text: Kilkenny's refuse dumped in Nore nightly?
